---
title: "Permutation or Combination? Decide Whether Order Matters"
description: "An interview maths technique with symbols, numbers and an independent proof."
---

## When this technique appears

When counting ways to arrange, select, split or order elements.

## The question

**Why does choosing two people differ from assigning first and second place?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
P(n,k)=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!},\quad {n\choose k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** n is the number of distinct objects; k is the number selected; ! is factorial, the product down to 1; P counts ordered selections and the binomial coefficient counts unordered subsets.

**Substitute actual numbers:** With n=4 and k=2, ordered pairs count 4×3=12. Unordered pairs count 12/2!=6 because each chosen pair appears in 2 different orders.

## Prove the mathematical step

First choose and order k distinct objects: n choices, then n−1, and so on. Every chosen unordered subset has k! orderings, so divide the ordered count by k! to count subsets.

## Common mistake or limitation

This assumes objects are distinct and selected without replacement. Repetition or duplicate objects changes the formulas.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: If swapping selected positions creates a new outcome, use permutations; otherwise divide by k!.**

Practise by speaking the argument, not reciting the formula alone.

**Interview problems:** Combinations; Permutations.

**Research reference:** [See the underlying method](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/binomial-coefficients.html). The worked examples and explanation are original.
